subject: English
description: Present participle (-ing), past participle (-ed/V3), perfect participle, dangling participle, participle as adjective.

questions.stem: In 'the BARKING dog scared the child', the word BARKING is a:
questions.explanation: PRESENT PARTICIPLE — verb form ending in -ING used as an ADJECTIVE describing a noun. 'Barking' modifies 'dog'. KEY DISTINCTION (the trickiest part): -ING words can be (1) GERUND — verb used as NOUN: 'BARKING is loud' (subject); 'I love BARKING dogs' (the gerund 'barking' acts as adjective here, but consider 'BARKING is annoying' = gerund as subject). (2) PRESENT PARTICIPLE — verb-derived adjective: 'the BARKING dog' (modifies dog). (3) CONTINUOUS TENSE auxiliary: 'the dog IS BARKING' (with 'to be'). PAST PARTICIPLE: -ED form (or V3) — 'a BROKEN window', 'the EXCITED child'. Indicates COMPLETED action or PASSIVE state. PERFECT PARTICIPLE: 'HAVING + V3' — 'HAVING FINISHED the work, she went home' (action completed before main verb). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES are more concise alternatives to 'WHO/WHICH/THAT' clauses: 'The man WHO IS RUNNING toward us' ≈ 'The man RUNNING toward us'. EXAM TRAP: 'dangling participle' — when participle's subject is unclear or wrong: 'Walking down the street, the building looked huge' (incorrect: building isn't walking). PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'The ___ window was repaired.' (something already broken)
questions.explanation: PAST PARTICIPLE = V3 — used as an adjective for COMPLETED actions or PASSIVE states. 'Broken window' = a window that has been broken. PARTICIPLE FORMS — three principal verb forms: (1) BASE (V1): break. (2) PAST SIMPLE (V2): broke. (3) PAST PARTICIPLE (V3): broken. REGULAR verbs: V2 = V3 (both add -ed): play/played/played, work/worked/worked. IRREGULAR verbs: V2 ≠ V3: break/broke/broken, see/saw/seen, run/ran/run, do/did/done, write/wrote/written. ADJECTIVE USAGE: -ED participle indicates SOMETHING THAT HAS HAD AN ACTION DONE TO IT (passive/completed). 'a frozen lake' (was frozen), 'an excited child' (became excited), 'a written agreement' (has been written). VS -ING (PRESENT PARTICIPLE) — active/ongoing: 'a freezing lake' (currently freezing), 'an exciting movie' (causing excitement), 'a writing pad'. KEY DISTINCTION trap: '-ed adjective describes what RECEIVES the action; -ing adjective describes what CAUSES the action.' 'Bored vs Boring' — 'I am bored' (someone made me bored); 'the lecture is boring' (it causes boredom). PYQ FREQUENCY: -ed/-ing distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct: 'The lecture was BORED / BORING.' (the lecture caused tedium)
questions.explanation: BORING (-ing) is used when the SUBJECT CAUSES the emotion: 'the lecture is BORING' (it makes me bored). BORED (-ed) is used when the SUBJECT FEELS the emotion: 'I am BORED' (the lecture made me bored). RULE: -ING describes the CAUSE of the feeling; -ED describes the EXPERIENCER of the feeling. COMMON PAIRS to memorize: (1) BORING/BORED. (2) EXCITING/EXCITED. (3) INTERESTING/INTERESTED. (4) AMUSING/AMUSED. (5) FRIGHTENING/FRIGHTENED. (6) AMAZING/AMAZED. (7) CONFUSING/CONFUSED. (8) DISAPPOINTING/DISAPPOINTED. (9) TIRING/TIRED. (10) FASCINATING/FASCINATED. EXAMPLES: 'The horror movie is FRIGHTENING' (it causes fear) vs 'the kids were FRIGHTENED' (they felt fear). EXAM TRAP: students often write 'I am boring' to mean 'I am feeling bored' — INCORRECT in formal English; 'I am boring' means 'I cause others to be bored'. KEY: subject-feeling sentences need -ED; description of stimuli use -ING. PYQ FREQUENCY: -ing/-ed feeling-adjective MCQs in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB English — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the dangling participle: 'Walking down the street, the building looked huge.'
questions.explanation: DANGLING PARTICIPLE — when the participial phrase doesn't logically connect to the SUBJECT of the main clause. The implied subject of 'walking' is missing or wrong. 'Walking down the street' should describe a PERSON, but the main clause's subject is 'the building' — buildings don't walk! CORRECT VERSIONS: (1) 'Walking down the street, I thought the building looked huge' (clear subject 'I'). (2) 'As I walked down the street, the building looked huge' (rewritten as a clause). (3) 'Walking down the street, I noticed the huge building' (subject and modifier match). MORE EXAMPLES of DANGLING participles: (a) 'Driving home, the moon was beautiful' (moon doesn't drive). (b) 'After studying for hours, the test was easy' (test doesn't study). (c) 'Tired and hungry, the dinner tasted great' (dinner isn't tired). RULE: the participial modifier MUST refer to the SUBJECT of the main clause. EXAM-FAVORITE: spotting dangling participles in SSC CGL Tier 2 error-spotting, IBPS PO Mains, CAT — 1-2× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests grammatical-logical alignment.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: '___ his keys, he searched the entire house.'
questions.explanation: PERFECT PARTICIPLE — formed with HAVING + V3. Used to indicate that the action of the participle was COMPLETED BEFORE the action of the main verb. 'Having lost his keys, he searched' = HE LOST KEYS FIRST, THEN SEARCHED. STRUCTURE: HAVING + V3 (past participle). EXAMPLES: (1) 'Having finished her work, she relaxed' (work done first). (2) 'Having read the report, the manager called a meeting'. (3) 'Having seen the movie before, I didn't want to watch it again'. CONTRAST: present participle 'LOSING his keys, he searched...' would imply CONCURRENT actions (he was losing AND searching at the same time — illogical here). PERFECT PARTICIPLE PASSIVE: 'HAVING BEEN + V3': 'Having been informed of the change, she adjusted her plans.' USE CASES: (1) Cause-effect: 'Having missed the bus, he was late'. (2) Time sequence: 'Having graduated, she joined a tech firm'. (3) Reason/justification: 'Having seen evidence, the jury convicted'. PYQ FREQUENCY: perfect participle in advanced English MCQs — CAT, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Identify the participle in: 'The water FLOWING from the tap was contaminated.'
questions.explanation: FLOWING is a PRESENT PARTICIPLE acting as an ADJECTIVE — modifies 'water'. The full noun phrase 'the water flowing from the tap' = 'the water THAT IS flowing from the tap' (relative clause shortened). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES are concise alternatives to relative clauses: 'the man WHO IS RUNNING' = 'the man RUNNING'. STRUCTURE: noun + participle phrase. EXAMPLES: (1) 'the boy SITTING on the bench' = 'the boy who is sitting'. (2) 'the dog BARKING loudly' = 'the dog that is barking loudly'. (3) 'the team WINNING the match' = 'the team that is winning'. NOTE: 'CONTAMINATED' in this sentence is a PAST PARTICIPLE used as a PREDICATE ADJECTIVE — describes the state of water. SO the sentence has TWO participles: 'flowing' (present participle modifying water) and 'contaminated' (past participle as predicate adjective). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES SAVE WORDS — make writing more concise. EXAM TIP: identify participles by looking for -ING or -ED/V3 forms acting as adjectives. PYQ FREQUENCY: participle identification in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Pick the correct form: 'The students ___ in the library are preparing for exams.'
questions.explanation: PRESENT PARTICIPLE 'STUDYING' — modifies 'students' (those who are currently studying). The phrase 'studying in the library' describes WHICH students. FULL EXPANSION: 'The students who are studying in the library are preparing for exams.' This is a PARTICIPIAL PHRASE replacing a 'who is/are + V-ing' relative clause. WHY NOT 'STUDIED'? Past participle implies COMPLETED action — but the sentence wants to describe ONGOING activity (students currently studying). 'Studied' would be passive: 'students studied in the library' = 'students who have been studied' (illogical). WHY NOT 'STUDY'? Base form requires auxiliary; 'who study' (relative clause) is grammatical but not a participial phrase. WHY NOT 'STUDIES'? That's the third-person-singular present (he/she studies); doesn't agree with plural 'students'. KEY METHOD: when describing an ONGOING ACTION done BY the noun, use PRESENT PARTICIPLE (-ing). When describing a COMPLETED ACTION done TO the noun, use PAST PARTICIPLE (-ed/V3). PYQ FREQUENCY: participial-phrase MCQs in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.
